one_liner: Official PUC Lua 5.4 compiled to WebAssembly with JS bindings; runs pure-Lua code about 10x faster than Fengari.
what_it_does: Embeds the real Lua 5.4 C VM (lua/lua, built with Emscripten) in Node.js, Deno and browsers, with a TypeScript layer that converts values between Lua and JS (tables, functions, promises via :await(), optional proxies of JS objects). On the npm 1.x API you create a LuaFactory, call createEngine(), then doString/doFile and global.get/set; the raw Lua C API is also exposed as lua.global.lua.*. It is not a drop-in for Fengari: Fengari exposes a JS reimplementation of the C API with Lua 5.3 semantics, wasmoon exposes Lua 5.4 and its own engine API, and the 2.0 pre-release renames the entry points (Lua.load(), createState()).
how_it_is_fast: Instead of interpreting Lua bytecode in JavaScript objects (Fengari), it runs PUC Lua's own C interpreter (luaV_execute, Lua's own GC and table code) as WebAssembly, so the VM loop is compiled ahead of time by clang/binaryen and then by V8's wasm tiers. Main builds use emcc -O3 with emmalloc and WASM_BIGINT; the 2.0 branches build with -Oz -fno-inline-functions and a gufa-optimizing binaryen pass for size. The cost moves to the JS/wasm boundary: every value crossing it goes through cwrap calls, string copies into linear memory and type-extension lookups.
when_to_use: Running compute-heavy Lua scripts (game logic, config evaluation, user scripting) inside Node.js, Deno or a browser where native Lua or a Node addon is not an option.
You need real Lua 5.4 semantics (integers, goto, to-be-closed variables, 5.4 standard library) rather than Fengari's Lua 5.3 reimplementation.
Long-running Lua code with few JS<->Lua crossings per unit of work, so the roughly 10x VM speedup is not eaten by marshalling.
Sandboxing: an instruction-count hook gives per-call timeouts (functionTimeout / run({timeout})) and an optional custom allocator caps Lua memory (traceAllocations with memoryMax).
when_not_to_use: Interop-heavy code (Lua calling many small JS functions or walking JS objects): the README warns the gain can vanish, and a third-party BabylonJS forum benchmark (search snippet only) had Fengari ahead on JS calls from Lua (13.3 vs 35.4, lower is better, units not given).

Bundle size matters more than speed: main README lists 393 kB plain / 130 kB gzipped vs Fengari's 214 kB / 69 kB, and the wasm file must be hosted or fetched (browser default loads glue.wasm from unpkg.com).
You need to await a Promise inside a JS-to-Lua callback or yield at a C boundary: README documents 'attempt to yield across a C-call boundary' and 'cannot resume dead coroutine' errors.
You want the fastest Lua possible on a server: native Lua or LuaJIT outside the JS engine will be faster, and no wasmoon-vs-native-Lua number is published.
Stable npm tooling matters: npm 'latest' is still 1.16.0 (2023-12-08), main stopped on 2025-01-18, and the 2.0 rewrite exists only as 2.0.0-next.0 and two feature branches.

integration.form: module (npm package with a separate glue.wasm; also a wasmoon CLI)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond the bundled glue.js/glue.wasm (@types/emscripten for typings); building needs Emscripten (or Docker emscripten/emsdk) and the lua/lua git submodule
integration.min_toolchain: Runtime: WebAssembly with BigInt integration (built with WASM_BIGINT); CI uses Node.js 22. Main is ESM-only since Jan 2025 (npm 1.16.0 predates that).
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host: Node.js, Deno, browsers, web workers; bundlers need fallbacks for path/fs/child_process/crypto/url/module (README)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each engine wraps one lua_State in one wasm instance, so treat it as single-threaded and use one engine per worker
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same Lua language (5.4 vs Fengari's 5.3) and a similar raw C API, but a different JS API, module loading and value-conversion layer

gotchas: The README's 25.5x (15.267 ms vs 389.923 ms) is one cold console.time run per VM in one process, Fengari first, so Fengari's JS tier-up is inside the timing. The project's own newer harness on the 2.0 branches (5 warm-ups, 100 iterations, fresh state per iteration, same heapsort.lua) reports 13.41 ms vs 137.36 ms average, 10.24x; the cold single run inflated Fengari's time about 2.8x (derived from page data).

Harness history and state: before commit c9d49bb (Nov 2022, issue #58 by gottfriedleibniz) the benchmark only loaded the chunk and never ran the sort (old table: 0.177 ms vs 2.107 ms on 20k numbers). At main HEAD, bench/comparisons.js and bench/steps.js still use require/__dirname, but package.json has been "type": "module" since 012fd13 (Jan 2025) with no bench/package.json, so they should fail with 'require is not defined in ES module scope' (code reading, not run). The table cannot be reproduced from main.

Both harnesses call the raw C API (luaL_loadstring + lua_callk/lua_pcallk) and bypass doString/thread.run and the type extensions that real users go through; no published number covers the interop layer.

npm 1.16.0 lacks main's later fixes (memory leak after running code on a new thread #109, Jan 2025); open issues include multi-return values (#84), JS constructors (#123), removing keys after interop (#82) and an alignment fault on close (#128). In src/thread.ts the timeout hook closure keeps the deadline it was first created with and is never released with removeFunction (code reading).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No other Lua-in-JS runtime is catalogued here; like markdown-wasm or libxml2-wasm it is the pattern of compiling the reference C implementation to wasm in place of a pure-JS port, and you pick it when you need real Lua 5.4 in a JS host. If you can run native code, the catalogued lua/lua itself is the faster choice.
verified_claims_summary: First-party only: on main, bench/heapsort.lua (ten heap sorts of 2,000 random numbers plus an order check, parse included) timed once per VM with console.time gave wasmoon 15.267 ms vs Fengari 0.1.4 389.923 ms (README, Nov 2022, ~25.5x); the 2.0 branches' warm 100-iteration harness gives 13.41 vs 137.36 ms (10.24x, Fengari 0.1.5). Neither table names the CPU, Node.js version or wasm build used (main's release build is emcc -O3, 2.0's is -Oz).
status_note: Main is quiet since 2025-01-18 and npm 'latest' is 1.16.0 from 2023, but development continues on the better-async-model and new-apis-2 branches (updated Sep 2026) with a 2.0.0-next.0 pre-release (2026-04-25); MIT-licensed and copyable, but expect API breaks in 2.0 and do not rely on main's bench scripts, which no longer run under the ESM package.
